definition: Artificial intelligence (AI) has a range of uses in government.
details: It can be used to further public policy objectives (in areas such as emergency services, health and welfare), as well as assist the public to interact with the government (through the use of virtual assistants, for example). According to the Harvard Business Review, "Applications of artificial intelligence to the public sector are broad and growing, with early experiments taking place around the world." Hila Mehr from the Ash Center for Democratic Governance and Innovation at Harvard University notes that AI in government is not new, with postal services using machine methods in the late 1990s to recognise handwriting on envelopes to automatically route letters. The use of AI in government comes with significant benefits, including efficiencies resulting in cost savings (for instance by reducing the number of front office staff) and reducing the opportunities for corruption. However, it also carries risks (described below).

explainer.lead: Artificial intelligence in government means using AI to deliver public services, pursue policy goals, and help people interact with public institutions. It can save time and money, but its benefits must be weighed against the risks of deploying it in government.

tiers.eli5: It is like giving a government office a very quick helper for certain jobs. One early example was reading handwriting on envelopes so letters could be sent to the right places automatically. Similar helpers can support public services or answer people's questions, but they can also create risks.
tiers.practitioner: Applications include emergency services, health and welfare, and virtual assistants for public interaction. A deployment may aim to reduce front-office workload and costs or limit opportunities for corruption, so efficiency gains should be assessed alongside the risks of government use.
tiers.paperLevel: AI in government is a broad application area rather than a single formally defined model or algorithm. It covers machine methods used for public policy objectives and citizen-facing interaction, with reported benefits including efficiency, cost savings, and reduced opportunities for corruption, alongside significant risks.

explainer.example: In the late 1990s, postal services used machine methods to recognise handwriting on envelopes. This allowed letters to be routed automatically rather than relying entirely on manual reading.

usedIn.name: Public-facing virtual assistants

explainer.intuition: Government can apply AI to both back-office work and public-facing services. The same use may offer greater efficiency while introducing risks that need consideration.
howItWorks: Identify a public policy objective or interaction that needs support.
Apply an AI method to a suitable task, such as recognising handwriting or assisting the public.
Use the result to support a service, such as routing a letter or answering through a virtual assistant.
Assess efficiency and cost savings alongside the risks of government use.
explainer.whyItMatters: AI can make government services more efficient, reduce staffing costs such as front-office work, and reduce opportunities for corruption. Those potential gains matter because government applications also carry risks.
misconceptions: AI in government is not entirely new; postal handwriting recognition was already in use in the late 1990s.
It is not only about virtual assistants; it also supports policy areas such as emergency services, health, and welfare.
Efficiency gains do not remove the need to consider its risks.
